 Government Affairs Report from NJBIA Post-Election Day Government Affairs Policy Committee Meeting
 Published 
 November 13
 SHARE
 Twitter
 Facebook
 LinkedIn
 NJBIA recently held a Government Affairs Policy Committee Meeting with the following guest speakers:
 Iris Delgado – Executive Director, NJ Democratic Assembly Campaign Committee 
 Daniel Bryan - Deputy Communications Director, Office of the Governor 
 Carlos Cruz – Vice President, Jamestown Associates 
 Luke Ferrante – Director, NJGOP 
 Ray Cantor – Deputy Chief Government Affairs Officer, NJBIA 
 Althea D. Ford – Vice President of Government Affairs, NJBIA 
 Jack Ramirez – Research Analyst, NJBIA 
 Jack Kelly – Policy Analyst, NJBIA 
 Chris Emigholz – Chief Government Affairs Officer, NJBIA 
 Here are some excerpts from the meeting:
 Iris Delgado (on Democrat Election Day takeaways): “Between every federal election cycle, more and more people get emboldened to become part of the process. In New Jersey, there are only 26 days from the day a candidate files for petition to when the first ballot is cast. And so that unfortunately causes additional strains in terms of communicating, messaging - all of that. That is something to consider in terms of how not only how DAC is planning, but how candidates approach elections. 
 “While there have been multiple wins – and I know that many people are talking about a more progressive side of the party – I think everybody can agree that ultimately, we all care about how to address affordability. I hope that that is the conversation that we'll have with voters starting today through Election Day next year, because that is the number one goal that not only the speaker has been focused on, but also our caucus in terms of everything that we do. 
 “We're going to have races that fit different buckets at different points throughout the year in terms of investments and execution – affordability is going to be the common thread throughout all of it.
 “In less than five years we are seeing early voting expand... About 53% of the electorate is going to have cast their ballot before Election Day even starts. It's a new perspective in terms of how everybody is approaching elections. That's one other thing that I would urge every organization that cares about the legislative races next year. The fact is that we can no longer wait until the week before Election Day to really start communicating with people.”   
 Daniel Bryan (on Democrat Election Day takeaways): “I think the result was a tsunami for a number of different reasons. If you look at what people said was important to them, it was affordability, right? That's something that everyone's been all talking about for years. 
 “But the number one topic was corruption... So many Democrats were talking about it. They didn't just say Trump's corruption, although they did point that out. They said the corruption on both sides down in Washington. And that's really what resonated.
 “So many millennial candidates in their late 30s and early 40s were coming and winning big, big races. Whether it's the two marquee races in New Jersey, whether it's Texas Senate, whether it's Ohio governor, whether it's Michigan Senate – all these big races were won by these younger candidates. 
 “So you really saw not only a partisan shift, you saw a generational shift on (Election Day). And I think a lot of that is just people just getting sick of the status quo. I think this was a very, very unique election cycle and we only know one or two chapters of the story right now. As the voter data comes out over the next month, I think it's going to tell a really interesting story.”
 Carlos Cruz (on Republican Election Day takeaways): “Tuesday was a nightmare. It represented a total shift of how we all should be thinking about the electorate. We've seen Hispanics go back and forth over the last few cycles. Largely, we took them for granted, and they spoke up and they spoke out and they showed up. 
 “This election isn't viewed neatly through a partisan lens. People broke free of their partisan shackles and of the camps and the boxes that we political consultants tend to neatly put them in.
 “I'm pleased to have worked for Kelly Ayotte in New Hampshire, who was one of the only folks to survive the blue tsunami and survive it pretty comfortably. The way we did that was by focusing on delivering. 
 “We liken affordability is a fun catch-all term, but then put a better point on it like it's delivering... It is not as simple as putting out a press release and saying, these are the things that we're doing. I think voters are ready for solutions and they're ready for people who are partners, and I think the Democrats made a great point of saying we are just as frustrated as you and we are your partners. Republicans focused on cultural war.”
 Luke Ferrante (on Republican Election Day takeaways): “The thing I want to highlight from my perspective was some local races where we found some success, where they bucked some of these trends. 
 “We have Mary Melfi, who has a great brand in Hunterdon County. Looking to next year, we're going to be holding the Democrats accountable. New Jersey's families are getting crushed. They're getting crushed for cost of living, utility rates and the state health benefit plan. We're excited to get started now that the dust is settling – recruiting candidates and building operations to carry us through next year.   
 Ray Cantor (on Climate Superfund Act): “If this bill were to pass, it would have a ripple down effect not only on cost, but on business expectations. When the government could place a major retroactive liability on companies that provide legal and necessary products, it would have a chilling effect on everything going forward. 
 “At this point, we believe that there's no intent by leadership to post the Climate Superfund bill for a vote. Obviously, nothing is permanent in this world and politics always change things. So, we're keeping a close eye on that.”    
 Ray Cantor (on the New Jersey Litigation Center): “NJBIA has just partnered with the New Jersey Civil Litigation Institute to form what we are calling the New Jersey Litigation Center. The new litigation center is going to allow us as a business community to be far more active in bringing first party suits when the legislature or a department has gone too far, without having to try to scrounge up the money each time we want to do so. 
 “Now we're going to have a real tool going forward to allow the business community to have a much better presence in the courts.”   
 Althea D. Ford (on education bill updates): “We are one of the members of the Public School Funding Formula Steering Committee, and so we've participated in the two meetings that have been held. 
 “There's been a lot of conversation obviously around funding and what that model should look like, but we continue to stay laser-cused on conversations that may compromise or challenge the 2% tax cap.
 “We do recognize that while there are pressures for trying to identify additional funding sources for our schools, we need to be mindful of that impact to not only the resident, but businesses that pay just under 50% of all property taxes.”
 “Second, I'll highlight that we participated in a childcare hearing. It was a joint committee about two weeks ago talking about the challenges and opportunities for the childcare industry. We are uniquely kind of situated in this conversation as we represent not only the childcare providers as businesses, many of them small, many of them women-owned. 
 “And so the challenges and opportunities that come with many of the initiatives that come from the state that negatively impact small business, but then we also have to manage the workforce challenges that result from a lack of reliable, accessible, affordable childcare options for employees. And so we're happy to continue participating in that work.
 Jack Ramirez (on AI bill updates): “The data center industry has supported 172,000 jobs across the state of New Jersey as it currently stands, and it has added an additional $30 billion into state, local and state and local tax revenue. So this is instrumental to our New Jersey economy... and NJBIA will be releasing some policy recommendations for the Legislature as they head into 2027.”   
 “I also wanted to highlight a few pieces of legislation that we're working on. S-4075 is an AI labor bill. This legislation monitors everything from employee hiring, firing, benefits that you give employees, scheduling, to the technologies utilized and as it currently stands, would capture things like Microsoft Teams, Excel, Word documents, anything of the sorts like that that utilizes machine learning... We think this is highly burdensome and it also affects our public employers.   
 “Lastly, one of the last things I wanted to talk about is A-5607. This is a privacy bill that deals with AI chatbots. I know that it is affecting a multitude of industries right now because there are no customer service exemptions – there's no B-to-B exemptions or anything of the sorts like that. It is a broad chat bot bill. 
 “We have a good brief document able to articulate the points of our members and highlight it. So we want to make sure that while we have this opportunity, we take advantage of it and highlight as much concern as possible.”   
 Jack Kelly (on labor and employment bill updates): “I am working on life post-ABC (test) being officially codified. We're pushing for a few different things. You can amend the tests and that will trump whatever's going on currently with the framework. You could cut out Prong B. You could align it with Pennsylvania law – they cut out Prong B and introduced additional factors for certain industries where misclassification is happening more than others.  
 "There also are a few carve-out measures that are sitting in the Legislature right now...   
 You have A-4735/S-4045 – that's an amateur sports official carve out. We have S-2782 for regulated professionals that were carved out under unemployment compensation law. And then you have a creative professionals carve out S-4715/A-5774.”   
 “Chairman Borrelli has a UI reporting bill that increases what's needed to be reported as well as the fines to for failure to comply. And Speaker Coughlin also has a UI reporting bill. It's weird that the labor chairs UI bill conflicts with the speaker's bill. We'll see which one takes the lead in that area. I don't necessarily think either of them are that great, but we need to dive into the weeds a little bit further on those.”   
 Chris Emigholz (on tax, budget, and economic development updates): “A $60.7 billion budget was signed. What's unique about that is a $60.7 billion budget was proposed by the governor back in early March and the first budget in a number of years where the signed number was pretty similar to the proposed number. A lot of that happened because we put some of the legislative spending in the supplemental appropriations bill.”   
 “We saw some investments in Governor Sherril’s saving time and money agenda. We saw some investments in manufacturing. We also saw some tax increases – $800 million in new taxes – which we were disappointed in seeing. Ultimately, that $800 million basically padded the surplus and was not necessary.”   
 “We're seeing positive things in manufacturing. Since we last met, the EDA has awarded 3 Next New Jersey manufacturing tax credits, which was a bill that NJBIA strongly supported last spring. Now, it's actually having dividends in the EDA and we're seeing new manufacturing jobs created.”
